content: Actaea racemosa, commonly known as black cohosh, black bugbane, black snakeroot, or fairy candle, is a flowering plant species belonging to the Ranunculaceae family. It is native to eastern North America, ranging from southern Ontario to central Georgia and extending westward to Missouri and Arkansas. This plant thrives in various woodland habitats and is often found in small woodland clearings. The roots and rhizomes of black cohosh have been used medicinally for centuries by Native Americans. Extracts derived from these plant materials are believed to have analgesic, sedative, and anti-inflammatory properties. Currently, black cohosh extracts are being investigated as potential treatments for symptoms associated with menopause. Black cohosh is a smooth, herbaceous perennial plant that grows from an underground rhizome. It produces large, compound leaves and can reach a height of approximately 25 inches. The basal leaves can grow up to 1 meter in length and width, forming repeated sets of three leaflets with coarsely serrated margins. The flowers, which bloom in late spring and early summer, are borne on tall stems and form racemes up to 50 centimeters long. These flowers lack petals and sepals, consisting instead of clusters of 55–110 white stamens surrounding a white stigma. The flowers emit a sweet yet fetid odor that attracts flies, gnats, and beetles. The fruit is a dry follicle, 5–10 millimeters long, containing several seeds. The taxonomic classification of black cohosh has been historically debated. Carl Linnaeus initially placed the species in the genus Actaea based on morphological characteristics of the inflorescence and seeds. However, Thomas Nuttall later reclassified it into the genus Cimicifuga, focusing on the dry follicles typical of Cimicifuga species. Recent morphological and genetic phylogeny analyses have demonstrated that black cohosh is more closely related to species in the genus Actaea than to other Cimicifuga species. Consequently, the species has been reclassified as Actaea racemosa, as originally proposed by Linnaeus. It is important to note that blue cohosh (Caulophyllum thalictroides), despite its similar common name, belongs to a different family (Berberidaceae) and is not closely related to black cohosh. Actaea racemosa thrives in consistently moist, heavy soils. It produces tall, tapering racemes of white midsummer flowers on wiry black-purple stems. The flowers have a mildly unpleasant medicinal odor, which is the origin of its common name bugbane. The drying seed heads remain visually appealing in gardens for weeks. The deeply cut leaves, particularly the burgundy-colored variety atropurpurea, add aesthetic interest to gardens, provided summer heat and drought do not cause the plant to die back. Black cohosh is a popular garden perennial and has received the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. Historically, Native Americans used black cohosh to treat gynecological and other disorders, including sore throats, kidney problems, and depression. It was included in the U.S. Pharmacopeia in 1830 under the name black snakeroot. In 1844, Dr. John King, an eclectic physician, popularized its use for treating rheumatism and nervous disorders. Other eclectic physicians in the mid-19th century used black cohosh for conditions such as endometritis, amenorrhea, dysmenorrhea, menorrhagia, infertility, severe postpartum pain, and to enhance breast milk production. In contemporary medicine, black cohosh is primarily marketed as a dietary supplement for women to alleviate symptoms of premenstrual tension, menopause, and other gynecological issues. Recent meta-analyses of clinical evidence support these claims. The design of studies and the dosage of black cohosh preparations influence clinical outcomes. Investigations into pure compounds found in black cohosh have identified beneficial effects on physiological pathways underlying age-related disorders, such as osteoporosis. However, there are concerns regarding the safety of long-term black cohosh use. According to Cancer Research UK, prolonged use may cause thickening of the uterine lining, potentially increasing the risk of uterine cancer. Individuals with liver problems are advised against using black cohosh, as it may cause liver damage. A 2011 meta-analysis suggested that this concern might be unfounded. Studies on human subjects administered commercially available black cohosh preparations did not detect estrogenic effects on the breast. However, no studies have evaluated the long-term safety of black cohosh use in humans. In a transgenic mouse model of cancer, black cohosh did not increase the incidence of primary breast cancer but did promote metastasis of pre-existing breast cancer to the lungs. Liver damage has been reported in a few individuals using black cohosh, although many women have taken the herb without adverse effects. A meta-analysis of well-controlled clinical trials found no evidence of adverse effects on liver function. Despite inconclusive evidence linking black cohosh to liver damage, Australia has mandated a warning label on all black cohosh-containing products, cautioning that it may harm the liver in some individuals and should not be used without medical supervision. Other studies suggest that liver damage from black cohosh use is unlikely and that the primary safety concern lies in the misidentification of plant materials and adulteration of commercial preparations with other plant species. Reported side effects include dizziness, headaches, seizures, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, sweating, constipation, low blood pressure, slow heartbeats, and weight issues. Black cohosh contains numerous bioactive organic compounds. Initially, estrogen-like compounds were thought to mediate its effects on vasomotor symptoms in menopausal women. However, subsequent studies have indicated the absence of estrogenic effects and compounds in black cohosh-containing materials. Recent findings suggest that some clinically relevant physiological effects of black cohosh may be due to compounds that bind to and activate serotonin receptors. A serotonin derivative with high affinity for serotonin receptors, Nω-methylserotonin, has been identified in black cohosh. Additionally, certain compounds, such as cycloartanes, have been shown to reduce cytokine-induced bone loss (osteoporosis) by inhibiting osteoclastogenesis in both in vitro and in vivo models.
